summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

primary_citations.citation_text: Montana - Title 41, Chapter 3 (Child Abuse and Neglect – mandatory reporting and protective services)

regulations_applicable.title: Department 37 - PUBLIC HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Rogers v. County of San Joaquin
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: A social worker who removed children without a warrant violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments where unsanitary home conditions, malnourishment and a child being locked in her room at night did not establish reasonable cause to believe the children faced serious bodily harm in the time it would take to obtain a warrant; reliance on factors closely tied to economic status would border on the unconstitutional.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Ninth Circuit's controlling statement of when protective custody may be taken without prior judicial authorization.
key_cases.quote: Thus, we hold that, under any view of the facts, the Rogerses' Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights were violated when Royal removed the children without a warrant.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Social workers who took a two-day-old from her mother in a hospital maternity ward without a warrant should have obtained one, but were entitled to qualified immunity because that obligation was not clearly established; summary judgment was reversed on the Monell claim because there was evidence the county maintained a policy of seizing children without warrants in non-exigent circumstances.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that a newborn under continuous hospital supervision is not in imminent danger, so protective custody there requires prior judicial authorization.
key_cases.quote: the social workers here lacked cause to forgo a warrant if they had adequate time to pursue one through the ordinary judicial process without risking B.W.'s well-being

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Dismissal of a mother's and daughter's familial-association claims on qualified immunity was reversed: taking a child from her mother at a hospital and continuing to detain her at a treatment center after professionals concluded she was a low suicide risk required reasonable cause to believe she faced imminent danger, and concern about the mother's lack of health insurance did not supply it.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that protective custody must end when the factual basis for imminent danger dissolves; continued detention is separately actionable.
key_cases.quote: Lack of health insurance, by contrast, does not provide a reasonable cause to believe a child is in imminent danger.

key_cases.holding: An interlocutory order granting temporary investigative authority and protective services is not appealable under Rule 1, M.R.App.P.; review must be sought by certiorari, habeas corpus or supervisory control, although the Court suspended the rules and reached the merits here because the parties had relied on a contrary prior statement.
key_cases.relevance: The TIA order here immediately removed the children into therapeutic foster care, showing the front-end custodial power the statute confers.
key_cases.quote: We hold, therefore, that an interlocutory order granting temporary investigative authority and protective services is not appealable under Rule 1, M.R.App.P.

key_cases.case_name: Wallis ex rel. Wallis v. Spencer
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for the City was reversed in substantial part: officials may not seize children on an uncorroborated account of abuse without first pursuing reasonable avenues of investigation, and absent a reasonable concern that physical evidence will dissipate or an urgent medical problem the state must notify parents and obtain judicial approval before subjecting a seized child to an investigatory physical examination.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that protective custody taken on a bizarre, uncorroborated third-party account, without any attempt to investigate it, cannot be defended as an emergency.
key_cases.quote: the police cannot seize children suspected of being abused or neglected unless reasonable avenues of investigation are first pursued

search_keywords: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services

state_agency.name: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, Child and Family Services Division

mandatory_reporters: Physicians, residents, interns, and hospital staff engaged in the admission, examination, care, or treatment of persons — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(a)
Nurses, osteopaths, chiropractors, podiatrists, medical examiners, coroners, dentists, optometrists, and any other health or mental health professionals — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(b)
School teachers, other school officials, and employees who work during regular school hours — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(d)

Social workers licensed pursuant to Title 37, child protection investigators, child reunification specialists, operators or employees of any registered or licensed day-care or substitute care facility, staff of a resource and referral grant program organized under § 52-2-711 or of a child and adult food care program, and operators or employees of a child-care facility — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(e)
Foster care, residential, and institutional workers — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(f)
Peace officers and other law enforcement officials — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(g)
Members of the clergy, subject to the confessional and canon-law exceptions — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(h), (6)(b)–(c)
Guardians ad litem and court-appointed advocates authorized to investigate a report of alleged abuse or neglect — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(i)
Employees of entities that contract with the department to provide direct services to children — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(j)
Department employees while in the conduct of their duties — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(k)

Added duty: a professional listed in § 41-3-201(2)(a) or (2)(b) who is involved in the delivery or care of an infant must report any infant known to the professional to be affected by a dangerous drug, as defined in § 50-32-101 — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(3)
reporting_details: Montana is not a universal-reporter state: only the professionals and officials listed in Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2) must report promptly to the department when, in their professional or official capacity, they know or have reasonable cause to suspect a child is abused or neglected, while § 41-3-201(4) allows any other person to report voluntarily.

statutory_basis.citation_text: Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-301(1)(a) — a child protection investigator, peace officer, or county attorney "who has reason to believe any child is in immediate or apparent danger of harm may immediately remove the child"; a district court must then find probable cause to continue the removal within 5 business days (§ 41-3-306(1)(a))

timeline_requirements.requirement_name: Written safety and risk assessment furnished
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Statute states no penalty; within 60 days the child protection investigator must furnish the written safety and risk assessment to the department and, on request, to the family (Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-202(6))
